title: BEEM: Boosting Performance of Early Exit DNNs using Multi-Exit Classifiers as Experts

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to improve early-exit (EE) inference by better utilizing information across exits, addressing the limitation that prior EE criteria treat every exit classifier equally and discard confidence from previous layers. Paper [4] discusses early exiting with ensemble internal classifiers but does not explicitly address the issue of leveraging confidence across exits. Paper [12] mentions that existing early exit methods ignore information extracted from previous exit layers, which aligns with the purpose of this contribution. Therefore, the purpose is **covered** by [12].

### Mechanism
The mechanism, BEEM, treats intermediate exit classifiers as experts in an ensemble, aggregating weighted confidence scores of consecutive previous exits whose predictions agree with the current exit. Papers [5], [9], [18], and [23] discuss weighted ensemble methods based on classifier confidence, which is substantively equivalent to the aggregation mechanism described here. Paper [4] also mentions ensemble internal classifiers but does not explicitly use weighted confidence aggregation across consecutive exits. Paper [12] proposes a Bag-of-Features-based method but does not use the same weighted aggregation mechanism. Paper [19] introduces an agreement rate initialized maximum likelihood estimator for ensemble aggregation, which is conceptually similar to weighting based on agreement. Thus, the mechanism is **covered** by [5], [9], [18], and [23].

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses GLUE (language tasks) and COCO (image captioning) benchmarks to measure speed-up and accuracy improvements. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [7], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [20], and [28] all evaluate early-exit methods using standard benchmarks and metrics for efficiency and accuracy, which matches the evaluation design. Although the specific benchmarks (GLUE and COCO) may differ, the evaluation design (speed-up and accuracy comparison against SOTA methods) is substantively equivalent. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered** by these prior papers.

### Domain
The domain is efficient inference/adaptive early-exit for transformer DNNs. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [7], [8], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [20], and [28] all work in the general area of efficient inference and adaptive early-exit for deep neural networks, including transformers. While some papers focus on specific sub-problems or architectures (e.g., vision transformers, edge computing), the general application area is the same. Therefore, the domain is **covered** by these prior papers.

I'll analyze each facet systematically against the prior papers.

---

**PURPOSE: Improve early-exit inference by better using information across exits, since prior EE criteria treat every exit classifier equally and discard confidence from previous layers.**

Paper [4] (Early Exiting with Ensemble Internal Classifiers) explicitly states: "Most existing work usually trains the internal classifiers independently and employs an exiting strategy to decide whether or not to exit based on the confidence of the current internal classifier. However, none of these works takes full advantage of the fact..." — this directly addresses the same gap: prior EE methods ignore information from previous exits.

Paper [12] also notes: "they ignore the information extracted from previous exit layers" as a limitation being addressed.

Both [4] and [12] share the same purpose: improve EE by leveraging information across multiple exits rather than treating each exit independently.

---

**MECHANISM: BEEM — treat each exit as an expert, aggregate weighted confidence scores of consecutive agreeing previous exits (deeper weighted higher), reset on disagreement, exit when aggregated confidence exceeds threshold.**

Paper [4] proposes using ensemble of internal classifiers for early exiting — treating internal classifiers as ensemble members. However, the specific mechanism of: (a) weighting by accuracy/cost, (b) consecutive agreement-based accumulation, and (c) reset on disagreement is more specific.

Paper [12] uses Bag-of-Features aggregating information from previous exits, but the mechanism is feature-level aggregation, not confidence-score weighted ensemble with agreement/reset logic.

Paper [6] (Early Exit Ensembles) uses ensemble of early exits for uncertainty estimation, treating exits as ensemble members — similar primitive of "exits as ensemble experts."

Paper [5] (Confidence in Prediction: Dynamic Weighted Ensemble) proposes dynamic weighted ensemble where classifiers are weighted by their confidence level — the same primitive of weighting ensemble members by confidence/accuracy.

Paper [18] proposes exponentially weighting probability estimates of base classifiers by cross-validated accuracy estimates — same primitive of accuracy-weighted ensemble aggregation.

Paper [26] (weight-adjusted voting algorithm for ensembles) — weighted voting based on classifier accuracy.

The agreement-based reset mechanism specifically echoes Paper [29]/[32] "The Value of Agreement, a New Boosting Algorithm" — using agreement among classifiers as a signal for weighting/boosting.

Paper [4] is the closest: it explicitly proposes using ensemble of internal classifiers for early exiting, treating exits as ensemble members and aggregating their predictions. The abstract says "none of these works takes full advantage of the fact" (that internal classifiers form a natural ensemble). The weighted aggregation with agreement/reset is a specific instantiation of this ensemble primitive, which is covered by [4] combined with weighted ensemble methods [5], [18], [26].

Paper [4] covers the core mechanism (ensemble of internal exit classifiers). The weighting-by-accuracy primitive is in [18] and [26]. The agreement-based weighting is in [29]/[32].

---

**EVALUATION: GLUE benchmark (NLP) and COCO (image captioning); speed-up metrics vs. final layer; comparison to SOTA EE methods.**

Paper [20] (DeeCap) evaluates early exiting on image captioning (COCO dataset) with efficiency metrics — same benchmark family (COCO) and same evaluation design (speed vs. accuracy tradeoff for EE).

Paper [2] (LECO) evaluates on GLUE with speed-up metrics comparing to SOTA EE methods — same benchmark family and metric semantics.

Papers [1], [3], [4], [8] all evaluate on GLUE with speed-accuracy tradeoff metrics for EE methods.

The evaluation design (GLUE + speed-up ratio + comparison to SOTA EE baselines) is covered by [2], [4], [8]; COCO captioning EE evaluation is covered by [20].

---

**DOMAIN: Efficient inference / adaptive early-exit for transformer DNNs.**

This is clearly covered by numerous papers: [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [7], [8], [11], [12], [15], [16], [17], [20] all operate in the same domain of efficient inference via early exiting in deep neural networks/transformers.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to set exit thresholds in a principled way with a guarantee of surpassing vanilla final-layer inference, addressing prior methods' lack of theoretical grounding and strong assumptions (e.g., equal error rate across layers). None of the prior papers explicitly address the theoretical grounding of threshold-setting for early exits with guarantees of surpassing vanilla inference. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [7], [9], [12], and [14] discuss early-exit mechanisms and efficiency improvements but do not focus on principled threshold-setting with theoretical guarantees. Paper [17] discusses reject option classifiers with bounded guarantees but does not address early-exit thresholds or the specific problem of surpassing vanilla inference.

### Mechanism
The contribution formulates threshold selection as a simple linear program using the error rates of the exit classifiers and derives a theoretical condition under which BEEM provably beats vanilla DNN inference. Paper [10] introduces linear programming for model selection, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism of using linear programming for threshold optimization. Paper [11] discusses threshold optimization for imbalanced data but does not use linear programming or derive theoretical guarantees. Paper [13] introduces automatic threshold tuning but does not use linear programming or address theoretical conditions for surpassing vanilla inference.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates that threshold-setting improves both speed-up and accuracy versus last-layer inference and derives a condition under which this improvement is guaranteed. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [7], [9], [12], and [14] evaluate early-exit mechanisms using similar designs, such as comparing speed-up and accuracy improvements against baseline inference methods. These papers use standard evaluation setups for early-exit models, including benchmarks and metrics for efficiency and accuracy, which match the evaluation design of this contribution. No new evaluation design is introduced here.

### Domain
The domain is efficient inference and early-exit threshold optimization. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [7], [9], [12], and [14] all operate in the same general application area of efficient inference and early-exit optimization. While this contribution may target a specific sub-problem, the domain itself is well-covered by prior work.

## PURPOSE

The purpose is: "Set exit thresholds in a principled way with a guarantee of surpassing vanilla final-layer inference, addressing prior methods' lack of theoretical grounding and strong assumptions (e.g. equal error rate across layers)."

Paper [9] ("Unsupervised Early Exit in DNNs with Multiple Exits") discusses exit point optimization and notes that "the last exit point may offer a better prediction error but also involves more computational resources." It addresses threshold setting but doesn't specifically focus on guaranteeing improvement over vanilla final-layer inference with theoretical grounding.

Paper [21] ("Optimization design of cascaded classifiers") presents optimization algorithms for cascade classifiers that "jointly optimize the setting of the thresholding parameters of all the node classifiers within the cascade" — this is principled threshold setting for cascaded inference, which is structurally similar. However, the specific purpose of guaranteeing improvement over vanilla (final-layer) inference is not the same objective.

Paper [17] ("Optimal strategies for reject option classifiers") derives optimal strategies with guarantees for selective classifiers, which is related but in a different problem class (reject option, not early exit).

Papers [20] and [24] address cascade classifier threshold optimization with principled methods, but their purpose is minimizing computation cost subject to detection/false-positive constraints, not guaranteeing improvement over a baseline final-layer classifier.

No prior paper specifically targets the purpose of providing a theoretical guarantee that early-exit threshold selection provably beats vanilla final-layer inference while addressing the equal-error-rate assumption. This appears uncovered.

## MECHANISM

The mechanism is: "Formulate threshold selection as a simple linear program using the error rates of the exit classifiers; derive a theoretical condition on intermediary-layer error rate under which early exit provably beats vanilla DNN inference."

Paper [21] ("Optimization design of cascaded classifiers") presents optimization algorithms for cascade threshold parameters — one of which is described as jointly optimizing thresholding parameters. However, it uses dynamic programming / greedy approaches, not a linear program formulation.

Paper [20] ("Optimally Training a Cascade Classifier") formulates cascade training as an optimization problem with constraints on detection/false-positive rates. This is close but uses a different optimization formulation (not LP over error rates).

Paper [24] ("Cascade Learning by Optimally Partitioning") formulates cascade learning as an optimization problem minimizing computation cost. Again, related but not LP over error rates.

Paper [10] ("Model Selection by Linear Programming") uses LP for model selection, but not for early-exit threshold setting.

The specific combination of (1) LP formulation over exit classifier error rates + (2) theoretical condition guaranteeing improvement over vanilla inference appears not directly covered by any prior paper.

## EVALUATION

The evaluation is: "Threshold-setting improves both speed-up and accuracy vs last-layer inference; a condition is derived under which this performance improvement is guaranteed (theoretical)."

The evaluation design involves comparing early-exit methods against vanilla final-layer inference on speed-accuracy tradeoffs, which is a standard evaluation design in early-exit literature. Papers [3], [5], [9], [14] all evaluate early-exit methods comparing speed-up vs. accuracy against baseline (final-layer) inference. This is a standard benchmark design in the domain.

Paper [9] specifically evaluates "An exit point that is 'optimal' in terms of both prediction error and computational resources" — comparing against last-layer inference.

The evaluation design (speed-accuracy tradeoff vs. final-layer baseline) is covered by multiple prior papers.

## DOMAIN

The domain is: "Efficient inference / early-exit threshold optimization."

This is clearly covered by numerous prior papers: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [9], [12], [14] all operate in the early-exit / efficient DNN inference domain.
